before.content_html:
Why Do Business Calculations Matter?

In the Edexcel GCSE Business exam, you will be expected to perform calculations without being given the formulas. Knowing the key formulas and understanding what the numbers mean is essential — not just for calculation questions, but also for “Discuss” and “Evaluate” questions where you need to interpret financial data and use it as evidence. This lesson covers the five core calculations: gross profit, net profit, gross profit margin, net profit margin, and average rate of return (ARR).

Key Fact

You will not be given formulas in the Edexcel exam. Quoting the correct formula before working through a calculation can earn you valuable marks, even if your final answer is slightly wrong.

Gross Profit

cost of sales includes the direct costs tied to the products being sold — the cost of buying stock from a supplier, delivery charges for that stock, and packaging. It does not include rent, wages, marketing, or other running costs.

The formula for gross profit is:

Key Fact

Gross Profit = Sales Revenue − Cost of Sales

A shop sells 400 hoodies at £28 each. The direct cost per hoodie is £15.

Step 1: Sales Revenue = 400 × £28 = £11,200

Step 2: Cost of Sales = 400 × £15 = £6,000

Step 3: Gross Profit = £11,200 − £6,000 = £5,200

If a business wants to increase gross profit, it can either raise its sales revenue (by selling more or increasing prices) or reduce its cost of sales (for example, by finding a cheaper supplier).

Net Profit

Net profit goes one step further than gross profit. It deducts operating costs (rent, salaries, insurance, marketing, utility bills) from gross profit to show the money that is actually left at the end.

The formula is:

Key Fact

Net Profit = Gross Profit − Operating Costs

Alternatively: Net Profit = Sales Revenue − Cost of Sales − Operating Costs

EuroParts sells 340 batteries at £125 each.

Sales Revenue = 340 × £125 = £42,500

Cost of Sales = £24,480

Gross Profit = £42,500 − £24,480 = £18,020

Operating Expenses & Interest = £14,450

Net Profit = £18,020 − £14,450 = £3,570

Despite strong gross profit, net profit is much lower because operating expenses consume most of the money.

Businesses often say net profit is the most important profit because it represents the money that is actually left. This leftover money can be paid to owners or shareholders, or reinvested back into the business to fund growth.

Gross Profit Margin (GPM%)

Gross profit margin tells you how much gross profit a business makes for every £1 of sales. It is expressed as a percentage, making it easy to compare performance over time or against competitors.

Key Fact

Gross Profit Margin (%) = (Gross Profit ÷ Sales Revenue) × 100

A GPM of 40% means for every £1 sold, 40p is gross profit and 60p covers the cost of sales.

A business has sales revenue of £18,500 and cost of sales of £13,690.

Step 1: Gross Profit = £18,500 − £13,690 = £4,810

Step 2: GPM = (£4,810 ÷ £18,500) × 100 = 26.00%

Companies use GPM to track performance over time, compare the profitability of different products, set prices, control direct costs, and check competitiveness against industry rivals. If GPM is falling, it could mean supplier prices have risen, the business is discounting too heavily, or it has shifted to selling lower-margin products.

Net Profit Margin (NPM%)

Net profit margin shows how much net profit a business makes for every £1 of sales after all costs have been paid — not just the direct cost of sales, but also operating costs like rent, wages, and marketing.

Key Fact

Net Profit Margin (%) = (Net Profit ÷ Sales Revenue) × 100

An NPM of 8% means for every £1 of sales, the business keeps just 8p as actual profit.

A business has sales revenue of £435 million, cost of sales of £315 million, and operating costs & interest of £95 million.

Step 1: Gross Profit = £435m − £315m = £120m

Step 2: Net Profit = £120m − £95m = £25m

Step 3: NPM = (£25m ÷ £435m) × 100 = 5.75%

This tells us that for every £1 of sales revenue, the business keeps only 5.75p as actual profit. Operating costs are consuming a large share of gross profit.

The key difference between GPM and NPM is what they measure. GPM shows how profitably a business is selling its products (are the direct costs under control?). NPM shows how well the business controls all its costs. A business could have a high GPM but a low NPM if its operating costs — such as rent, wages, or marketing — are very high.

Average Rate of Return (ARR)

When a business has limited money and several possible investment projects, it needs a way to compare them. The average rate of return (ARR) calculates how profitable an investment will be relative to its cost, expressed as a percentage.

Key Fact

ARR (%) = (Average Annual Profit ÷ Cost of Investment) × 100

The 3-step method: (1) Add up all annual profits and divide by the number of years to get average annual profit. (2) Divide average annual profit by the initial cost. (3) Multiply by 100 to get a percentage.

Jacksons PLC is comparing two investment options:

Project A — Extend existing factory. Cost: £60m. Lifespan: 25 years. Total profit expected: £720m.

Step 1: Average Annual Profit = £720m ÷ 25 = £28.8m

Step 2 & 3: ARR = (£28.8m ÷ £60m) × 100 = 48.00%

Project B — Purchase new equipment. Cost: £90m. Lifespan: 40 years. Total profit expected: £2,250m.

Step 1: Average Annual Profit = £2,250m ÷ 40 = £56.25m

Step 2 & 3: ARR = (£56.25m ÷ £90m) × 100 = 62.50%

Project B has the higher ARR (62.50% vs 48.00%), so based purely on the numbers, it would be the better investment. It also generates income for 40 years compared to just 25 years for Project A.

The project with the highest ARR percentage is usually the one a business should choose because it generates the greatest return on the money invested. However, ARR is based on predicted profits, which may turn out to be inaccurate, and it does not account for when the profits arrive — getting money sooner is generally better for cash flow.

Interpreting Financial Data

Calculations alone are not enough — the exam also tests your ability to interpret what the numbers mean. When you compare financial data across two time periods or two businesses, always look at the trend and explain why the figures have changed.

A clothing shop has sales of £120,000 this year with a GPM of 30%. Next year, sales rise to £140,000 but GPM falls to 25%.

This year: Gross Profit = 30% of £120,000 = £36,000

Next year: Gross Profit = 25% of £140,000 = £35,000

Despite sales revenue increasing by £20,000, gross profit actually fell by £1,000. This suggests the business is facing higher direct costs, offering more discounts, or has shifted to selling lower-margin products. Rising revenue does not always mean rising profit.

When interpreting data in the exam, state the calculation, identify the change or trend, and then explain a possible reason. Common mistakes include calculating correctly but then failing to say what the result actually means for the business.

practice_questions.marks:
1 mark(s) for a clear definition:
• The percentage of sales revenue that is net profit (1).
• It shows how much profit a business keeps from every £1 of sales after all costs have been paid (1).
Do not accept just 'the profit a business makes' without reference to sales revenue or percentage.

practice_questions.text: Outline one reason why a business would calculate the gross profit margin rather than just gross profit.
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks for identifying, 1 mark for development:
• Gross profit margin is expressed as a percentage (1), which makes it easier to compare performance over time or against businesses of different sizes (1).
• It shows how much of every £1 of sales is kept as gross profit (1), helping the business judge whether its pricing and direct costs are competitive (1).

practice_questions.text: A business has sales revenue of £50,000 and cost of sales of £30,000. Calculate the gross profit and the gross profit margin.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Gross Profit = SR – CoS = £50,000 – £30,000 = £20,000 (1 for formula, 1 for correct answer).
• GPM = (GP ÷ SR) × 100 = (£20,000 ÷ £50,000) × 100 = 40% (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why net profit is often considered more useful than gross profit when judging business performance.

1 marks for identifying, up to 2 marks for explanation/development:

practice_questions.text:
Shultz & Sheiff make small petrol engines. They are considering two growth options.

Option 1: Extend existing factory. Cost: £18m. Lifespan: 20 years. Total profit: £140m.
Option 2: Relocate to new factory with new equipment. Cost: £26m. Lifespan: 45 years. Total profit: £540m.

Discuss which option Shultz & Sheiff should choose. Use calculations to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks across knowledge, application, and analysis:

Option 1 ARR:
• Average Annual Profit = £140m ÷ 20 = £7m (1)
• ARR = (£7m ÷ £18m) × 100 = 38.89% (1)

Option 2 ARR:
• Average Annual Profit = £540m ÷ 45 = £12m (1)
• ARR = (£12m ÷ £26m) × 100 = 46.15% (1)

Analysis/Discussion:
• Option 2 has a higher ARR (46.15% vs 38.89%), so it generates a better return per pound invested (1).
• However, Option 2 costs £8m more upfront and requires relocating (recruiting new staff, losing experienced workers, relying on road upgrades). Option 1 keeps existing skilled staff and avoids disruption (1).
• On the other hand, Option 2 generates income for 45 years vs 20, and the new equipment allows quality assurance which could reduce waste (1).

Accept other valid points about risk, cash flow, qualitative factors.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate whether a business with high gross profit margin but low net profit margin is performing well. Justify your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Lower band (1-3): Limited understanding. Identifies that the business makes money from sales but has high costs, with little explanation.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Sound understanding. Explains that high GPM means the business prices well or has low cost of sales, but low NPM suggests operating costs (rent, wages, marketing) are eating into profit. May give an example.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Thorough analysis. Discusses both sides – the business is strong at its core activity (buying/selling) but weak at controlling overheads. Uses examples of operating costs. May discuss whether this is a short-term issue (e.g. just opened a new store with high rent) or a long-term structural problem.
Top band (10-12): Evaluative judgement. Weighs up both sides and reaches a justified conclusion. For example: 'Overall, the business is not performing well because it does not matter how much gross profit you make if operating costs consume it all – net profit is what pays dividends and funds reinvestment. However, it depends on context – a new business may accept low NPM while it builds market share, and the high GPM shows the product itself is profitable, so reducing operating costs could quickly improve performance.' Must use terminology accurately and consider context.

before.content_html:
Organisational Structures

Every business needs a clear structure so employees know who they report to, what their responsibilities are, and how decisions flow through the organisation. An organisational structure is a diagram that shows the hierarchy of a business — who is in charge, who reports to whom, and how the business is divided into departments or teams.

Key Fact

Key vocabulary for organisational structures: the chain of command is the line of authority from top to bottom; the span of control is the number of subordinates a manager is directly responsible for; delegation is giving a task to a lower-level employee; and delayering is removing one or more layers of management to cut costs and speed up communication.

Hierarchical vs Flat Structures

A hierarchical structure has many layers of management. Authority flows from the top down through a long chain of command. Managers typically have a narrow span of control, meaning they supervise only a small number of employees. This means they can get to know their team well and delegate tasks effectively.

However, communication in a hierarchical structure can be slow because messages must pass through many layers. This can make the business inflexible and slow to respond to changes in the market. It is also expensive because there are more managers and supervisors to pay.

A flat structure has few layers of management and a short chain of command. Managers have a wide span of control. Communication is faster because there are fewer levels for messages to travel through. Employees are often given more responsibility and autonomy, which can be motivating.

The downside is that staff can become overstretched because there is less supervision. Wide spans of control mean managers may lose touch with individual employees, and power struggles can develop when the manager is not around.

In a centralised organisation, decisions are made at head office by senior management. This ensures consistency but can be slow and may not respond well to local customer needs. In a decentralised organisation, decision-making power is given to managers and employees closer to the customers. This speeds up decisions and gives local staff more responsibility, but it can lead to inconsistency across the business.

The Recruitment Process

Recruitment is the process of finding and hiring the right person for a job vacancy. It follows a clear seven-stage process that ensures the business finds the most suitable candidate.

Key Fact

The seven stages of recruitment: (1) identify the vacancy, (2) write a job description (duties and responsibilities), (3) write a person specification (qualifications, skills, and qualities needed), (4) advertise the vacancy, (5) receive applications and CVs, (6) interview shortlisted candidates, (7) offer the job and issue a contract.

There are different job roles within a business hierarchy. Directors sit at the top and make strategic long-term decisions. Senior managers are appointed by the board to run day-to-day operations. Supervisors and team leaders oversee small teams of workers. Operational staff carry out the core work of the business, while support staff help the business function (for example, ICT technicians or teaching assistants in a school).

Internal recruitment means filling a vacancy with someone already working in the business. It is cheaper (no advertising costs), quicker (no induction needed), and less risky because the candidate’s track record is known. However, it limits the pool of applicants and may cause resentment among staff who are not chosen.

External recruitment means hiring someone from outside the business. This brings fresh ideas and new skills, which can help the business innovate. However, it is more expensive (advertising, interviews, induction) and riskier because the candidate is unknown.

Training and Development

Training is the process of teaching employees new skills or improving existing ones. Businesses that invest in training benefit from higher productivity, better quality work, and a more motivated workforce.

Formal training is structured, with set objectives, often delivered by an outside expert. It may lead to a qualification (for example, a food hygiene certificate) but is expensive and takes employees away from their work.

Informal training takes place on the job, where a colleague shows the employee how to do something. It is cheap and quick but may not be as thorough.

Self-learning means studying without a teacher, for example through online courses. Ongoing training ensures employees continuously develop their skills to keep up with industry changes and new technology.

Businesses also use target setting and performance reviews to develop employees. Targets should be SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Timely). Performance reviews are formal meetings between an employee and their supervisor to discuss progress, set new targets, and identify training needs.

Key Fact

There is a direct link between training, motivation, and retention. Employees who receive regular training feel valued and are more motivated. Motivated employees are less likely to leave, which reduces recruitment costs and maintains productivity. Retraining is especially important when new technology is introduced.

Motivation Theories

Understanding what motivates employees helps businesses improve productivity and reduce staff turnover. Three key theorists are studied at GCSE level.

Taylor believed that workers are primarily motivated by money. He argued that managers should observe workers, break tasks into small steps, and find the most efficient way to do each task. Workers should then be paid piece rate — the more they produce, the more they earn. While this can boost output, it ignores the fact that many workers care about more than just pay, and repetitive tasks can be demotivating.

Maslow’s hierarchy of needs arranges human needs in five levels: (1) physiological — basic needs like food and shelter (met by wages); (2) safety — job security and safe working conditions; (3) social — belonging, teamwork, and friendships at work; (4) esteem — recognition, praise, and promotion; (5) self-actualisation — reaching your full potential through challenging and creative work. According to Maslow, each level must be satisfied before a person can move to the next.

Herzberg identified two sets of factors. Motivators actually increase job satisfaction and include achievement, recognition, interesting work, responsibility, and promotion. Hygiene factors do not motivate on their own, but their absence causes dissatisfaction — these include pay, working conditions, company policy, and relationships with colleagues. According to Herzberg, improving hygiene factors only prevents unhappiness; to truly motivate employees, businesses must provide motivators such as challenging work and opportunities for growth.

Key Fact

Taylor focused on money as the key motivator (piece rate). Maslow said workers have a hierarchy of five needs from basic survival to self-fulfilment. Herzberg distinguished between motivators (which create satisfaction) and hygiene factors (which only prevent dissatisfaction). In the exam, you need to be able to compare these theories and apply them to business scenarios.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the likely impact on a business of changing from a hierarchical structure to a flat structure.
practice_questions.marks:
Lower band (1-2): Elements of knowledge and understanding, e.g. identifies that communication may improve or that managers will have wider spans of control.
Mid band (3-4): Accurate knowledge and analysis in context. Chains of reasoning, e.g. fewer layers means communication is faster, this means decisions can be made more quickly, as a result the business can respond faster to market changes.
Top band (5-6): Detailed analysis with balanced consideration. Both advantages (faster communication, lower wage costs from delayering, more employee responsibility) and disadvantages (managers overstretched with wider span of control, loss of supervision, possible redundancies causing low morale) are explored with developed chains of reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate whether financial methods of motivation, such as piece rate pay, are always the most effective way to motivate employees. Justify your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Lower band (1-3): Limited knowledge shown, e.g. identifies that money can motivate workers or mentions one theory.
Mid band (4-6): Good application of knowledge with some analysis. Discusses Taylor’s view that money motivates, and contrasts with Maslow or Herzberg. For example, Herzberg argued pay is only a hygiene factor — it prevents dissatisfaction but does not create motivation. Maslow suggested workers have higher needs like esteem and self-actualisation that money alone cannot fulfil.
Top band (7-9): Detailed, balanced evaluation with a justified conclusion. Weighs up financial methods (piece rate, bonuses, profit sharing) against non-financial methods (recognition, training, job enrichment, teamwork). Concludes with a justified judgement, e.g. ‘Financial motivation is important for meeting basic needs, but Herzberg’s research suggests that long-term motivation requires challenging work and recognition. The most effective approach depends on the type of business and its workforce.’
